messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Curriculum Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 33

**Vignette: Kofi, Age 30**

Kofi grew up believing that love was something you fought for — not literally, but with patience, with loyalty, with showing up. That belief is part of what kept him in the relationship with Marcus for nearly two years, long after the first time Marcus's hand connected with the side of his face during an argument over something neither of them can now remember. Kofi told himself it was an isolated incident. Then he told himself it wouldn't happen again. By the third time, he had stopped telling himself anything at all.

The physical violence was unpredictable in the way that made it most corrosive — not constant, but always possible. A raised voice, a shift in Marcus's posture, the particular way he went quiet before he didn't — Kofi learned to read these signals the way he now reads curriculum frameworks: carefully, searching for patterns, trying to anticipate what comes next. He left the relationship eighteen months ago, after Marcus shoved him into a kitchen counter hard enough to fracture two ribs. A colleague noticed him wincing at his desk and asked. He told her he'd fallen. She didn't push. He was grateful and ashamed in equal measure.

Kofi works as a curriculum designer for a nonprofit that develops educational materials for secondary schools across West Africa. He is good at his job — methodical, creative, deeply committed to the idea that the right sequence of learning can change how a young person understands the world. His colleagues describe him as calm and thoughtful. What they don't see is that he sometimes sits at his desk for twenty minutes without opening a single file, his mind somewhere else entirely, replaying a scene he can't edit or revise. He has missed two project deadlines in the past six months, which is unlike him, and he has started declining invitations to collaborative workshops because the thought of being in a room where someone might raise their voice — even in enthusiasm — makes his chest tighten in a way he can't easily explain.

He lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment and prefers it that way, for now. He has not been on a date since leaving Marcus. When friends suggest setting him up, he deflects with humor, and he is convincing enough that most of them believe him. He doesn't entirely believe himself. At night, sleep comes reluctantly and leaves early. He wakes sometimes at two or three in the morning with his heart already going fast, the details of a dream dissolving before he can name them, leaving only the feeling — that particular combination of smallness and dread that he associates with standing in Marcus's kitchen, trying to read the room.

What troubles Kofi most, and what he finds hardest to say aloud, is the self-questioning. He is a man. He is, by most external measures, capable and composed. He grew up in a household where his father was the one who raised his voice, and his mother was the one who absorbed it, and somewhere in that history he absorbed the idea that men do not end up in situations like the one he was in. That belief has made it difficult to name what happened to him clearly, even to himself. He sometimes catches himself minimizing it — *it wasn't that bad, other people have it worse* — and then catches himself minimizing, which is its own exhausting loop.

He has recently started journaling, not because anyone suggested it but because he spends his professional life believing in the power of structured reflection. He writes mostly questions. He is not yet sure what the answers look like. He knows, in the careful and honest part of himself, that something was taken from him — some ease in the world, some basic assumption that the people who say they love you will not also hurt you — and that getting it back is going to require more than time.
